opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that what we see today with something like Codex CLI is a pretty early snapshot of where this is going.

Right now the dominant mode is very interactive and fairly synchronous. You're sitting in your terminal, you give the agent a task, it reads some files, proposes some changes, runs some commands, and you're kind of watching over its shoulder and steering it. That's genuinely useful, and for a lot of people it's the right entry point, because it builds trust. You can see what the model is doing and catch it when it goes off the rails.

But I think the direction things are heading is toward much more asynchronous, delegated work. Instead of pairing with one agent on one task, you'll be more like a tech lead or a manager who hands off a bunch of tasks in parallel. Go fix this bug, go write tests for this module, go investigate why this service is flaky. Those agents go off and work in their own environments, sometimes for a long time, and come back with something reviewable, like a pull request with an explanation of what they did and why, and evidence that it works.

A few things have to get better for that to really work. One is the length of the horizon the model can operate on reliably. Today agents are pretty good at tasks that take minutes; the frontier is pushing toward tasks that take hours, and that requires the model to plan, recover from its own mistakes, and know when it's actually done versus when it just thinks it's done.

The second is verification. The bottleneck shifts from writing code to reviewing code. If an agent produces ten PRs while you were in a meeting, you need ways to trust them without reading every line, so better testing, agents that check other agents' work, clearer summaries of what changed and what the risks are.

The third is context about your organization. A lot of what makes a senior engineer valuable isn't raw coding ability. It's knowing why the code is the way it is, what the team's conventions are, what was tried before and didn't work. Agents that can pick up that institutional knowledge and remember it over time are going to be dramatically more useful than ones that start from scratch every session.

And then finally I think the interface itself evolves. The terminal is a great home for developers, but the agent will increasingly live wherever the work happens: in your issue tracker, your code review tool, your Slack, your CI pipeline. You might not even think of it as "opening the agent." It's just a teammate that's always there and picks up work.

So the short version is: from a tool you drive to a collaborator you delegate to. The human role doesn't go away. It shifts toward defining what good looks like, setting direction, and making judgment calls, while more of the execution gets handed off.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents taking multiple delegated tasks, working independently for extended periods, and returning reviewable pull requests while the user is occupied.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that Codex CLI today is kind of a snapshot of what the technology can do right now, and the thing that I find myself telling people is that the interface is almost a reflection of the model's current abilities rather than some end state we're aiming at.

So today, the pattern is very much: you sit in your terminal, you give the agent a task, you watch it work, you review the diff, you approve or you don't. That's a synchronous, one-on-one, pair-programming kind of relationship. And that's appropriate for where the models are, because they still make mistakes often enough that you want a human in the loop pretty tightly.

But I think there are a few directions this goes as the models get better.

The first is that the unit of work gets bigger. Right now people hand off tasks that take the agent a few minutes. As reliability goes up, you start handing off tasks that take hours, and that changes the interaction model entirely. You're not watching it anymore. You're delegating. You come back and you review the result the way you'd review a pull request from a colleague. And that's actually a big part of why we have both the CLI and the cloud version of Codex, because the cloud version is a bet on that asynchronous, many-agents-at-once future where you're kicking off a bunch of things in parallel and triaging the results.

The second is that the agent stops being confined to the code. Writing code is honestly the easy part. The hard part of being a software engineer is understanding what to build, reading the ticket, looking at the logs, reproducing the bug, running it in a staging environment, talking to the person who filed the issue. So I think coding agents evolve into something more like engineering agents, where they have access to all of those surrounding tools and context, and the code change is just one step in a longer workflow.

The third thing, and this is the one I'm maybe most excited about, is that the agent gets better at knowing when to ask. One of the failure modes today is the agent either barrels ahead on an ambiguous spec and produces something that's confidently wrong, or it asks too many clarifying questions and you'd rather have just written it yourself. Getting that calibration right, knowing which decisions matter enough to check in on and which ones a senior engineer would just make, is a huge part of what makes a human engineer trustworthy. And I think that's a capability we can actually train for.

And then the last piece is that the interface itself probably dissolves a bit. The terminal is where developers live today, so that's where we started. But I don't think the future is necessarily "you type into a CLI." It's more that the agent shows up wherever the work is, whether that's your editor, your issue tracker, your CI system, or a Slack thread, and the terminal becomes one surface among many.

So the short version is: longer-horizon tasks, broader access to the engineering environment, better judgment about collaboration, and less dependence on any single interface. The CLI is a great place to learn what works, but I'd be surprised if it looked the same in two years.

r001.rationale: The candidate says users will delegate longer tasks, stop watching the agent work, and return later to review its result.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re going to move from agents that you interact with very closely, one task at a time, toward agents that you can delegate larger pieces of work to. Today, you’re often in the loop saying, “Make this change,” looking at the result, and then figuring out what to ask next. Over time, the agent should be able to take more responsibility for that whole process: understanding the problem, making a plan, implementing it, and checking whether it actually worked.

The key is that checking step. Writing code is only part of software engineering. You need to run tests, interpret failures, and sometimes use the product to see whether the behavior makes sense. The more effectively an agent can get that feedback for itself, the longer it can work independently.

So I imagine the interaction becoming more asynchronous. You hand off a task, the agent works on it, and it comes back with something you can review—or with a specific question when it needs your judgment. Then your role becomes more about defining what success looks like and making the decisions that require context the agent doesn’t have.

r001.rationale: The response describes handing off a task for the agent to work on independently and return for review, with interaction becoming more asynchronous. This conveys that the user can leave the agent to complete delegated work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll move from agents that you interact with one prompt at a time to agents that can take on a larger chunk of work independently. Instead of saying, “Change this function,” you’ll describe an outcome, and the agent will explore the codebase, make a plan, implement it, run tests, and iterate based on what it finds.

The hard part is giving the agent a way to know whether it’s actually succeeded. Writing code is one piece, but checking that the behavior is right often requires running the application, looking at the interface, or understanding constraints that weren’t explicit in the original request.

So I imagine the developer’s role becoming more about specifying the goal, providing that context, and reviewing the important decisions. You’ll still want a tight feedback loop, but you won’t necessarily need to supervise every individual step.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents handling larger tasks independently with less step-by-step supervision, but does not say the user can work on something else while the agent completes the work.
